units: the writer is keeping the dog of a close friend who has gone traveling
the animal whined at night behind the bedroom door
it refused to eat its ration
it damaged the floor with its claws whenever she moved away
the writer first read this behavior as a reproach
a training specialist explained that the animal was looking for a steady reassuring landmark
she was advised to keep the outings regular and to put the bedding near the entrance
the dog now sleeps against a cloth that carries the smell of its owner
text: Your dog stayed with me while you were away, and I am writing at last with the relief of someone who has found the way out. The first nights were bad. He whined behind my bedroom door, left his ration untouched, and raked the floorboards with his claws the moment I stepped away from him. I took it as a reproach for your leaving. Then a trainer set me straight: the animal was hunting for a steady landmark, not for a punishment he had earned. She told me to walk him at the same hours every day, to hang his lead where his nose could reach it, and to push his bedding against the wall by the front door. He settles there now as soon as the light goes, curls into the cloth that still holds your smell, and waits for the lock to turn without a sound. He eats, he runs, he sleeps hard. You will find a calm companion, and a friend rather pleased with herself.

units: specialists in animal behavior refuse to treat the two kinds of group as one thing
in a herd of grazing animals each beast adjusts to its nearest neighbors
no member of that group holds an overall view of the movement
among bees the scouts come back and pass on directions through their movements
the colony keeps the site that gathers the most support
the first group exchanges body postures and changes of pace
the second group exchanges content comparable to a reasoned proposal
the first reacts almost instantly while the decision of the second takes several days
text: Ask whether a herd and a swarm run on one and the same machinery, and researchers who study animal behavior will tell you no. In a herd, every beast trims its own path to the ones moving beside it, and the shape of the whole comes out of nothing but those local corrections. No single animal holds the plan of the movement. A swarm works on another principle altogether. Scouts fly back and spell out directions through the way they move, and the colony settles on the site that draws the most backing. So what separates the two systems? The kind of signal each one carries. A herd passes along a stance, a burst of speed, the turn of a head. A swarm passes along content, something close to a case being argued. And what about speed? A herd answers within a fraction of a second. A swarm weighs the matter for days on end before it lifts off.

units: a livestock keeper set out her worries to a veterinary practitioner
she reported that the animals had been eating less grass for a week
she added that the chewing of the cud lasted less time than usual
the practitioner examined the teeth of the animals
he then checked the quality of the water on offer
he also judged the fodder too poor in fiber
he recommended keeping the weakened animals apart from the group
he promised to come back and check the state of the herd
text: The keeper laid out her worries to the vet who had come to look over her animals. She told him her cows had been grazing less for a week, that they stopped chewing the cud earlier than usual, and that one had lain down in the middle of the pasture. The practitioner answered that he would work through three leads in order. He began with the teeth of each animal, since one broken tooth is enough to put a cow off her chewing. He moved on to the trough, drawing water from a pipe that struck him as fouled. He finished with the fodder, which he judged too poor in fiber and badly suited to their digestion. Before leaving, he advised her to keep the weakened animals apart, to note every refusal of feed, and to call his office if intake did not climb back. He promised to come by again and check the herd.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the coming together of humans and wild animals began with a mutual acceptance
predators came to look for the waste left around the camps
the least fearful individuals ended up being fed
hunting groups mixing humans and dog like animals took shape
grazing animals were then penned as a living store of meat
those beasts were sorted for their calm and for their fleece
the rise of crops created a need for animals able to pull loads
cats were tolerated to keep rodents away from the grain stores
text: Domestication begins with no decision at all. It begins with a truce that neither side ever spelled out. Meat eaters prowled the edges of the hunting camps, drawn by the scraps thrown aside there. The warier ones bolted at any noise. The bolder ones lingered, and in the end they were fed by hand. Out of that closeness came the mixed pack, human and animal running down the same game together. Next came the penning of grazing beasts, held at first as meat kept alive, then picked over for a quiet temper and for a thick fleece. Tilled ground raised a demand of another kind, and the sturdiest animals were harnessed to drag the loads. Later, cats were suffered in the grain stores, where they held the rodents off the harvest. Every stage lengthened the list of species bound to us, and reshaped their bodies as much as their tempers.

units: one sometimes finds on the ground a thin see through casing left by a reptile
the outer layer of a snake skin does not stretch as the animal grows longer
that stiffness forces the reptile to get rid of its old casing
a fresh layer builds up underneath the old one
a fluid slips between the two layers and lifts them apart
the eyes of the animal turn cloudy during this phase
the snake hunts little and stays hidden while its sight is poor
it rubs its snout against a stone to start the peeling
text: Ever picked up one of those see through husks at the edge of a path and wondered what animal could have left it lying there? That is a snake skin, and the whole business comes down to a simple flaw in the design. The casing that shields the reptile will not stretch. It stays stiff while the animal underneath keeps getting longer. So it has to shed. A fresh layer builds up below, then a fluid works its way between the two and lifts them apart. While that is going on, the eyes turn a milky blue and the snake can barely see a thing. So it hardly hunts, and tucks itself away under a stump. Once the split is complete, it scrapes its snout against a rough stone, catches the lip of the old casing, and crawls straight out of it the way you peel off a sock. What you find lying on the ground is that worn out coat.

units: a print left in the mud near a pen set off the alarm
ewes had been killed during the night
the sheep farmers blamed the losses on a wild meat eater
a naturalist judged the print too broad for that idea
cameras that fire on movement were put in place
the pictures showed two dogs running loose without an owner
the owners of the dogs were traced and held to account
an electrified fence and a night watch put an end to the attacks
text: The alarm went up over a single print in the mud, a few steps from a pen where three ewes had been killed during the night. Sheep farmers up the valley named a wild meat eater at once, and asked for leave to go out and shoot it. The naturalist sent to the spot refused to sign off on that. The pad printed in the mud looked too broad to her, and the bites sat wrong for a practiced killer. On her word, cameras that fire on movement were strung along the fences and left there. The pictures, collected a week later, showed two dogs running loose across the field, collars still around their necks. Their owners were traced without much trouble and held to account for the losses. The local council paid for an electrified fence and for a watch through the dark hours, and the killing stopped dead.

units: two ways exist of watching wild birds
the first is to put out food that draws them in
this way quickly brings the bolder species close
it changes the behavior of the birds one claims to study
the second is to sit motionless inside a screen of branches
it demands staying quiet through a long wait
it shows behavior that food never brings about
it is advised to begin with the first way and then take up the second
text: Before you carry your binoculars down to the hedge, settle on one of the two ways of coming at birds, because they will hand you very different things. The first lays out bait: a scatter of seed on a board, a lump of fat tied to a low branch. The bolder species turn up fast, counting them is easy, and what you end up watching are guests at a table rather than free birds. The second asks you to build a screen of branches, to sit down inside it before first light, and to hold still. The wait runs long and the cold creeps in through everything you wear. In return you catch the display, the squabble over a dry stem, the heavy flight of a bird carrying nest material home. Start with the bait until the shapes are familiar. Move to the screen once the names come to you without a pause.

units: a team of researchers is finishing the yearly count of a sea bird colony
the count covers occupied nests and not the adults in view
the breeding numbers have fallen against the previous campaign
the fish these birds live on has moved into deeper water
the adults range further out to feed
the eggs are left alone more often than before
gulls take advantage of these absences to plunder the nests
the team recommends limiting the access of walkers to the foot of the cliffs
text: A team of researchers has wrapped up the yearly survey of a colony lodged on the coastal cliffs, and their findings come in four parts. Numbers first. The count rests on occupied nests, a steadier measure than the adults in view at any one moment, and the total has dropped sharply against the previous campaign. Feeding next. The fish the species lives on has moved into deeper water, which stretches out every trip the birds make. Breeding after that. The adults range further from the rock, eggs sit uncovered that ought to be brooded, and gulls with an eye for the gap plunder the exposed nests. Access last. The team urges closing the foot of the cliffs to walkers through the sensitive weeks, a modest step by its own account, but one that can be taken without any delay at all.

units: the mare leaves her stall when the gate opens
she halts and reads the air before going on
she shakes her whole coat to rid it of the damp
she rolls on her back in a sandy hollow
she eats the grass of the pasture for a long stretch
she heads for the trough set under a tree
she stays on her feet and dozes in the shade of the leaves
she waits near the rail for someone to come and bring her in
text: The moment the gate swings open, the mare steps clear of her stall and stops, nostrils flared, to read the air of the pasture. She goes three paces on, then shakes herself from crest to tail until the damp of the night leaves her coat in fine drops. The roll follows. She folds her forelegs, tips onto her flank, works her back into a sandy hollow, and rises with a thrust of the loins. Then she grazes without lifting her head, moving in short even shifts along the fence, tearing at the rich growth of the margins and passing over the coarse tufts of the middle, until the heat turns her toward the trough standing under the tree. There she drinks, stays on her feet, one hind leg resting, eyelids heavy, ears turning. Late in the day she comes back to the rail and waits, still, for someone to lead her in.

units: wildlife parks justify their existence by the saving of species
their opponents hold that confinement unmakes the animals
the ground on offer is far smaller than the range covered in freedom
this restriction brings on repeated movements in meat eaters
the food handed out removes any active searching
animals born in captivity survive badly once released
the writer proposes keeping these parks for species genuinely at risk
the writer suggests funding the protection of wild habitat with the gate money
text: Wildlife parks defend themselves by pointing to the species they save. Their critics answer that confinement unmakes the very animal it claims to shield. The argument deserves to be followed to its end, because one effect pulls the next along. An enclosure, however generous, offers ground that bears no comparison with the range a meat eater covers when it is free. Out of that shrinkage come the mechanical journeys back and forth along the bars, familiar to every keeper. Food handed over at fixed hours then wipes out the search, and with it any schooling in the hunt. It follows that beasts born behind a grille rarely last long when they are turned back into the wild. The conclusion holds, to my mind. Keep these parks for species genuinely at risk, and turn the gate money over to the defense of wild habitat.
